title: Acute stroke: conditional complete reporting/curriculum structure requirement draft

reporting_checklist.label: Haemorrhage
reporting_checklist.detail: Inspect parenchyma, subarachnoid spaces and extra-axial compartments before describing ischaemia.

reporting_checklist.label: Parenchyma
reporting_checklist.detail: Localise early change or diffusion restriction by side, arterial territory and strategic structures.

reporting_checklist.label: Occlusion
reporting_checklist.detail: Name artery and segment, tandem cervical disease and distal reconstitution.

reporting_checklist.label: Collaterals
reporting_checklist.detail: State acquisition type, distribution and delay relative to the opposite side.

reporting_checklist.label: Tissue and complications
reporting_checklist.detail: Report available core/delay estimates, mass effect, hydrocephalus and relevant alternative diagnoses.

reporting_template_sections.heading: BRAIN PARENCHYMA
reporting_template_sections.body: Acute ischaemic change: [absent / present / indeterminate]; side/territory [ ]. Involved structures [ ]. ASPECTS if applicable [__/10]; regions [ ]; modality [ ].

reporting_template_sections.heading: HAEMORRHAGE
reporting_template_sections.body: Intracranial blood: [absent / present]; compartment/site [ ]; extent [ ]. Haemorrhagic transformation [absent / petechial / haematoma / not applicable].

reporting_template_sections.heading: ARTERIAL FINDINGS
reporting_template_sections.body: Occlusion [none / artery and segment]; tandem lesion [ ]. Cervical arteries [ ]; distal reconstitution [ ]; relevant stenosis/dissection [ ].

reporting_template_sections.heading: COLLATERALS AND PERFUSION
reporting_template_sections.body: CTA phase [single / multiphase]; collateral description [ ]. Perfusion [not acquired / valid / limited]; software/thresholds [ ]; core __ mL; delayed tissue __ mL; mismatch [ ].

reporting_template_sections.heading: MASS EFFECT AND OTHER FINDINGS
reporting_template_sections.body: Midline shift __ mm; basal cisterns [ ]; ventricles [ ]; herniation [absent / specify]. Alternative explanation or incidental actionable finding [ ].

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old presents with sudden dysphasia and right arm weakness. On the unenhanced CT the left middle cerebral artery looks dense - but so do the right middle cerebral artery, the basilar artery and the superior sagittal sinus, and the brain parenchyma looks unremarkable. The haemoglobin is 197 g/L. What best accounts for the dense vessels?
choices: A high haematocrit raising attenuation throughout the vessels
Thrombus filling the left middle cerebral artery trunk
Mural calcification of the intracranial vessel walls
Iodinated contrast retained from a recent study
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: A high haematocrit raising attenuation throughout the vessels
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: The discriminator is symmetry and company. A thrombus is one clot in one artery, so the sign is unilateral and is judged by comparing the vessel with its fellow on the same slice; a raised haematocrit raises the attenuation of blood itself, so arteries, veins and dural sinuses rise together, and a dense superior sagittal sinus alongside dense arteries is the giveaway that the finding is in the blood rather than in one lumen. Mural calcification is denser still and sits as a rim in the wall, following the vessel rather than filling it, and it is usually bilateral and irregular. Retained contrast would opacify the vessels far more brightly and would come with a history. The trap in the last sentence of the stem is the normal-looking parenchyma: at ninety minutes a normal brain is entirely compatible with a large ischaemic core, so it argues for proceeding to CT angiography rather than for reassurance.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: An unenhanced CT two hours after onset of a right hemiplegia shows early ischaemic change in the left insular ribbon, the left lentiform nucleus, and the cortical regions M1, M2 and M5. Every other region of the scoring template is normal. What ASPECTS does this study score? Answer with the number alone.
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: ASPECTS starts at 10 and subtracts one point for each of ten regions showing early ischaemic change: caudate, lentiform, internal capsule, insular ribbon and the cortical regions M1 to M3 at the ganglionic level, and M4 to M6 at the level just above the ganglia. Five involved regions leaves 5. The score matters because it stands in for core volume when perfusion imaging is unavailable, and the early-window thrombectomy trials enrolled largely at 6 or above, which is still where the guideline recommendation is strongest. Since 2023, SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT and RESCUE-Japan LIMIT have shown benefit in large cores down to an ASPECTS of about 3, so a low score is now a reason for discussion rather than an automatic exclusion. Two cautions in scoring: count established hypoattenuation or focal swelling rather than a subjective impression, and do not count an old infarct as new.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: Ninety minutes after a middle cerebral artery occlusion the diffusion-weighted images are unmistakably abnormal while the unenhanced CT of the same territory looks close to normal. Account for the difference in terms of where the water is.
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: Arterial occlusion causes energy failure within minutes, the sodium-potassium ATPase stops, and sodium and water move from the extracellular space into the intracellular compartment. This is cytotoxic oedema: total tissue water is barely changed, but water has been redistributed into a compartment where its Brownian motion is hindered, so the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) falls and the DWI signal rises. CT attenuation tracks total tissue water content, which has hardly altered at this stage; it falls only later, once ionic oedema and then breakdown of the blood-brain barrier draw new water into the tissue from the vasculature, which is why frank hypoattenuation lags the diffusion change by hours.
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: The two studies are sensitive to different physical quantities, and that is the whole answer: diffusion imaging is sensitive to where water is, CT to how much of it there is. Knowing the time course keeps the reader out of two traps. The ADC falls immediately, reaches its nadir over the first days, pseudonormalises at around a week to ten days as cell lysis and vasogenic oedema raise diffusivity again, and then rises above normal; so a bright DWI with a normal or high ADC late on is T2 shine-through rather than new ischaemia, and a subacute infarct can look deceptively unimpressive on diffusion alone. At the front door the corollary is blunter: a normal CT does not exclude infarction and is not a reason to withhold treatment, whereas a normal DWI in the first hours makes infarction unlikely, with small brainstem lesions and profound hypoperfusion imaged before a core has formed as the exceptions worth remembering.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old wakes at 07:00 unable to speak, having been well at 22:00 the night before. MRI at 08:30 shows a left middle cerebral artery territory lesion that is bright on diffusion-weighted imaging with a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and no corresponding signal change on FLAIR. What does the discrepancy between the two sequences allow you to say?
choices: The lesion is probably less than about 4.5 hours old
The lesion is probably more than twelve hours old
The lesion is an artefact of a poor diffusion trace
The lesion is chronic and unrelated to the symptoms
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: The lesion is probably less than about 4.5 hours old
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: Diffusion turns positive within minutes, while FLAIR signal follows the rise in tissue water and becomes visible at roughly 4.5 to 6 hours; a lesion that is bright on diffusion but invisible on FLAIR therefore dates itself to the first hours. That mismatch is what the WAKE-UP trial used to select patients with an unknown onset time for thrombolysis, and it found benefit. Here the clock reads nine hours since last seen well and the tissue reads under four and a half - the tissue wins. The near-miss is 'more than twelve hours old', which runs the logic backwards: by twelve hours the FLAIR abnormality would be conspicuous, and a DWI lesion with matching FLAIR change is the appearance that argues against a hyperacute onset. A low ADC is what separates a true diffusion lesion from T2 shine-through, so it is quoted in the stem deliberately.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A patient with a suspected large-vessel occlusion arrives nine hours after last being seen well, and the hyperacute protocol runs from the scanner to the angiography suite. Put these acquisitions in the order the protocol performs them.
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: The unenhanced study comes first and answers one question - is there blood? - because everything downstream, thrombolysis above all, depends on that answer, and the same images supply the ASPECTS. CT angiography is second, because finding the occlusion, and seeing the aortic arch and cervical vessels the catheter must travel through, decides whether thrombectomy is possible at all. Perfusion is third and is a selection tool rather than a diagnostic one: in the late window it separates a small core with a large penumbra from a completed infarct. Catheter angiography is last and is part of the treatment. Running perfusion before angiography spends contrast and minutes on a question that only matters once a target exists, and leaving the unenhanced study until last is how a haemorrhage gets thrombolysed.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: CT perfusion nine hours after onset gives an ischaemic core, defined as relative cerebral blood flow below 30 per cent of the contralateral side, of 25 mL, and a Tmax greater than 6 s volume of 90 mL. What is the mismatch ratio? Give it to one decimal place.
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: The mismatch ratio is the whole critically hypoperfused volume divided by the core, 90 over 25, which is 3.6; the mismatch volume - tissue at risk but not yet lost - is the difference, 65 mL. DEFUSE 3 selected patients 6 to 16 hours from last seen well with a core under 70 mL, a ratio of at least 1.8 and a mismatch volume of at least 15 mL, and this patient clears each criterion comfortably. DAWN worked out to 24 hours using a clinical-core mismatch instead, pairing age and NIHSS against core volume. Two cautions travel with these maps: Tmax above 6 s marks critically delayed tissue rather than tissue certain to die, and in very early presentations the core map overstates the damage, so a large core in the first couple of hours deserves scepticism rather than an automatic exclusion.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old is found with weakness of the left leg much worse than the left arm, with the face spared, and is apathetic and incontinent of urine. Before the images are reviewed, which arterial territory should be scrutinised first?
choices: The right anterior cerebral artery territory
The right middle cerebral artery territory
The right posterior cerebral artery territory
The right anterior choroidal artery territory
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: The right anterior cerebral artery territory
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: The homunculus does the work. Leg and perineum lie on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery; face and hand lie on the convexity, which belongs to the middle cerebral artery. A leg-dominant deficit that spares the face is anterior cerebral until proved otherwise, and the apathy and incontinence fit the same vessel, since the medial frontal cortex and anterior cingulate share its supply. Middle cerebral occlusion gives face-and-arm weakness with aphasia or neglect; posterior cerebral gives a homonymous hemianopia and, when the thalamus goes, hemisensory loss; the anterior choroidal artery gives hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia from the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the optic tract, without cortical signs. One corollary: isolated anterior cerebral infarction is uncommon, and bilateral medial frontal infarction should prompt a look for an azygos anterior cerebral artery or for vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A 69-year-old smoker has repeated brief episodes of right arm weakness, worse on standing up. MRI shows a chain of small acute infarcts in a line through the left corona radiata between the lateral ventricle and the cortex, and CT angiography shows a 90 per cent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Which mechanism does the pattern of the infarcts favour?
choices: Failure of perfusion in the internal borderzone
Artery-to-artery embolism to cortical branches
Lipohyalinosis of a single lenticulostriate vessel
Cardioembolism to the middle cerebral trunk
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: Failure of perfusion in the internal borderzone
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: Geometry is the argument. The internal borderzone lies in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale, at the far end of the deep perforators and the penetrating pial arterioles - the last field the water reaches. When perfusion pressure falls behind a tight carotid stenosis, infarcts appear there as a rosary of lesions strung in a line, and the postural trigger for the symptoms is the clinical half of the same observation. Embolic infarcts scatter across different territories, sit at the grey-white junction and take wedge or scattered cortical shapes rather than a straight line; a single lacune from lipohyalinosis is one lesion, not a chain. The distinction changes treatment: a haemodynamic pattern behind a symptomatic 90 per cent stenosis argues for prompt revascularisation and for caution about dropping the blood pressure, whereas an embolic pattern shifts attention to the plaque surface and to the heart.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old taking a combined oral contraceptive has had three days of worsening headache and then a seizure. Unenhanced CT shows patchy haemorrhage with disproportionate surrounding oedema in both high parietal lobes, and the superior sagittal sinus looks dense. What does this combination point to?
choices: Venous infarction from dural sinus thrombosis
Bilateral anterior cerebral artery infarction
Haemorrhagic contusions from unwitnessed trauma
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: Venous infarction from dural sinus thrombosis
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: The pattern breaks the rules that arterial infarcts obey. Parasagittal lesions on both sides correspond to no single arterial territory; they are haemorrhagic early rather than late; and the oedema is out of proportion to the lesion because the mechanism is back-pressure rather than absent supply. Add a dense sinus and the diagnosis is venous. Confirm with CT or MR venography, where the empty delta sign is a filling defect within the enhancing sinus wall, and remember that a dense sinus alone can be nothing more than a high haematocrit. Bilateral anterior cerebral infarction, possible with an azygos vessel, would follow the medial surface forward from the genu of the corpus callosum and would not be haemorrhagic at three days. Contusions cluster at the skull base against the orbital roofs and sphenoid ridges. PRES sits posteriorly, parieto-occipital, and is predominantly vasogenic oedema. The management consequence is the striking part: the treatment is anticoagulation, in the presence of intracranial haemorrhage.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A patient with a large right middle cerebral artery infarct has a routine CT at sixteen days. The territory that was clearly hypoattenuating on day two now looks close to normal, and the report concludes that the infarct has resolved. Explain what has happened to the tissue, and how you would answer the report.
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: This is the fogging phase. Between roughly the second and fourth week, macrophages infiltrate the infarct and new capillaries proliferate within it, so its attenuation rises back towards that of normal brain and the lesion becomes inconspicuous on unenhanced CT. The tissue is not recovering; it is being cleared, and the encephalomalacic cavity will appear later. The report should be answered by saying that a transiently normal-looking CT in this window is not evidence of resolution: the infarct remains demonstrable on MRI, where it stays abnormal on T2 and FLAIR, and it will enhance on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI because the blood-brain barrier is broken.
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: Fogging is worth knowing because it appears exactly when the follow-up scan tends to be booked, and because it can hide a subacute infarct in a patient scanned late for the first time: a normal CT two weeks after an event is not evidence that no stroke occurred. The mechanism is the one that also produces gyriform cortical enhancement and, on MRI, cortical T1 hyperintensity from laminar necrosis at around two weeks - reperfused, infarcted cortex packed with macrophages. The trap on the other side is calling that subacute infarct a tumour, since it enhances and can show mass effect. What keeps the reader right is the shape and the history: a wedge that respects a vascular territory and reaches the cortical surface, in a patient whose deficit began on a known day.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: A 77-year-old with atrial fibrillation was last seen well fourteen hours ago and has an NIHSS of 18. There is no haemorrhage, the ASPECTS is 8, CT angiography shows an occluded left M1 segment, and perfusion gives a core of 12 mL with 95 mL of critically delayed tissue. The on-call team proposes medical management because the six-hour window has passed. What is the strongest response?
choices: Imaging, not the clock, selects patients out to 24 hours
The scan should be repeated after twelve more hours
Intravenous thrombolysis alone is the option left
The core is too large for an endovascular approach
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: Imaging, not the clock, selects patients out to 24 hours
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: DAWN and DEFUSE 3 replaced the clock with a tissue clock, and guidelines followed: thrombectomy is recommended out to 24 hours from last seen well in patients who meet imaging criteria. This patient meets them with room to spare - an ASPECTS of 8, a 12 mL core and 95 mL of penumbra fourteen hours in, which is the imaging signature of a slow progressor with good collaterals. 'The core is too large' inverts the numbers on the screen. A repeat scan buys nothing except infarct. Intravenous thrombolysis is outside its own window here (4.5 hours, extended to 9 hours only in perfusion-selected patients in trials such as EXTEND), and in any case thrombolysis is not a prerequisite for thrombectomy. The practical lesson is that in the late window the question is never 'how long has it been?' but 'how much brain is still alive?'.

literal_curriculum_quiz.prompt: Two patients each have an occluded M1 segment, an NIHSS of 16, and presented three hours after onset. On multiphase CT angiography the first fills the pial vessels of the affected hemisphere almost as well and almost as fast as the normal side; the second shows sparse and delayed pial filling. Explain what the difference predicts and how it should change what you do next.
literal_curriculum_quiz.answer: Collateral supply through the pial or leptomeningeal anastomoses determines how fast penumbra converts into core. The first patient is a slow progressor: at three hours the core will still be small and the penumbra large, the chance of a good outcome after successful thrombectomy is high, and there is time to complete the imaging properly and to transfer if the centre cannot treat. The second is a fast progressor whose core is already growing quickly, may already be large despite the short time from onset, and for whom every minute of delay costs tissue, so imaging should be curtailed to what is needed to get the patient onto the angiography table. Collateral status is also why time from onset predicts core volume so poorly, and why a late presenter with good collaterals can be a better candidate than an early one with poor collaterals.
literal_curriculum_quiz.explain: Collaterals are the variable that makes the same occlusion a different disease in two patients. They are graded on the extent and the timing of pial filling relative to the normal hemisphere, and multiphase CT angiography exists because a single-phase study confuses a slow-filling good collateral bed with an absent one - the phase was simply caught too early. Good collaterals predict a smaller final infarct, a better functional outcome and a lower risk of haemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion; poor collaterals predict the opposite and are the reason some patients arrive early and are already beyond help. Two things follow for practice: report collateral status rather than only the occlusion site, and treat a poor collateral pattern as a reason to compress the workflow rather than as a reason to give up, since the tissue that remains is exactly the tissue that will be lost during any delay.
